title: Exploring network structure, dynamics, and function using NetworkX
venue: Proceedings of the 7th Python in Science Conference (SciPy 2008)
key_finding: Presents NetworkX, a Python package for studying network structure and algorithms: data structures for many graph types (incl. directed graphs and self-loops), nodes as any hashable object with flexible attribute data, algorithms for metrics such as shortest paths, centrality and clustering, generators for classic models (Erdos-Renyi, small-world, Barabasi-Albert), and integration with SciPy (abstract via OpenAlex, paraphrased by fetch tool).

title: scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment
key_finding: Docs state the implementation is 'a modified Jonker-Volgenant algorithm with no initialization, described in ref. [2]', where [2] = D.F. Crouse, On implementing 2D rectangular assignment algorithms, IEEE TAES 52(4):1679-1696, Aug 2016, DOI 10.1109/TAES.2016.140952 (=D07). Ref [1] is Wikipedia 'Assignment problem'. Added in version 0.17.0.
limitations: SciPy does NOT implement Kuhn's (1955) Hungarian method per se; cite D06 for the problem/method history and D07 for the actual algorithm. No complexity statement on page.
notes: Page title 'linear_sum_assignment — SciPy v1.18.0 Manual'; version 1.18.0; accessed 2026-10-04. Author attribution 'The SciPy community' is conventional for SciPy docs (not printed in fetched text).

title: scipy.stats.wilcoxon
key_finding: 'Calculate the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.' Defaults: zero_method='wilcox' (discards zero differences), alternative='two-sided'; 'pratt' and 'zsplit' alternatives for zeros. method in {'auto','exact','asymptotic'} or PermutationMethod; 'auto' uses exact for n<=50 and asymptotic otherwise; with ties or zeros 'exact' no longer computes the exact p-value and 'auto' uses exhaustive permutations when len(d)<=13, asymptotic otherwise. References include Wilcoxon 1945 (pp. 80-83), Pratt 1959, Conover 1971, Cureton 1967.
limitations: Behaviour is version-specific (1.18.0); report the SciPy version and zero_method used in experiments.
notes: Page title 'wilcoxon — SciPy v1.18.0 Manual'; accessed 2026-10-04. The n<=50 threshold wording is from the fetch tool's summary of the method parameter; ties/zeros sentence quoted from Notes.

key_finding: CP-SAT-LP (Google OR-Tools) implements a purely integral CP solver on top of a SAT solver using Lazy Clause Generation, integrates simplex/LP and MIP techniques and scheduling algorithms, and uses a portfolio of diverse workers (incl. local search and LNS) for search, reported as state-of-the-art/competitive.

title: The Hungarian method for the assignment problem
key_finding: Defines the assignment problem (assign n persons to n jobs to maximise total score) and shows that ideas latent in the work of two Hungarian mathematicians yield a new solution method.
limitations: Foundational; SciPy's linear_sum_assignment uses a modified Jonker-Volgenant algorithm (D07), not Kuhn's original procedure.
notes: All draft fields confirmed; issue '1-2' added (OpenAlex). Published 1955-03.

title: On implementing 2D rectangular assignment algorithms
venue: IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems
key_finding: Reviews research on the 2D rectangular assignment problem and combines the best methods into a k-best 2D rectangular assignment algorithm with bounded runtime; identifies the 'best' algorithm as a strongly polynomial shortest-augmenting-path approach; Matlab code provided. Cited by SciPy docs as the basis of linear_sum_assignment (D03a).

title: There's plenty of room at the Top: What will drive computer performance after Moore's law?
key_finding: Multiplying two 4096x4096 matrices took 25,552.48 s (~7 h) in Python vs 2,372.68 s in Java (10.8x) and 542.67 s in C (47x); fully optimised parallel/vectorised C took 0.41 s (62,806x). 'Java and C avoid the extraneous work that Python does under the hood to make programming easier'; 'The price for this performance gain is programmer productivity: Coding in C is more onerous than coding in Python'. Post-Moore performance gains must come from software, algorithms and hardware architecture.
limitations: Single dense numeric kernel in pure Python loops; does not measure NumPy/SciPy-vectorised code or graph workloads.
notes: Discovered for D17. Metadata via OpenAlex (date 2020-06-04; issue date 5 Jun 2020 on PDF). Full text read from author copy hosted by Microsoft Research. Author initials follow OpenAlex display names (Neil Thompson, Butler Lampson, Daniel Sánchez); fuller initials not confirmed.

title: time — Time access and conversions (time.perf_counter)
key_finding: perf_counter() returns 'the value (in fractional seconds) of a performance counter, i.e. a clock with the highest available resolution to measure a short duration'; includes time elapsed during sleep; reference point undefined so only differences are valid; on CPython uses the same clock as time.monotonic() (changed in 3.13). Added in 3.3; perf_counter_ns() added in 3.7. process_time() returns system+user CPU time of the process, excluding sleep.
limitations: Wall-clock measure; sensitive to system load. Pin Python version.
notes: Accessed 2026-10-04; page version 3.14.8. No publication date on page (year null).

title: tracemalloc — Trace memory allocations
key_finding: 'The tracemalloc module is a debug tool to trace memory blocks allocated by Python' (added 3.4). start() installs hooks on Python memory allocators; get_traced_memory() returns (current, peak) size of traced blocks; reset_peak() (added 3.9) sets peak to current. Storing more frames increases memory and CPU overhead.
limitations: Traces only allocations via Python's allocators (memory allocated outside them, e.g. by some C extensions, may not be counted - inference from 'allocated by Python', not stated explicitly in fetched text); tracing adds overhead, so do not time and trace in the same run.
notes: Accessed 2026-10-04; page version 3.14.8.

title: random — Generate pseudo-random numbers
key_finding: Python uses the Mersenne Twister core generator (53-bit precision floats, period 2**19937-1). Notes on Reproducibility: reusing a seed reproduces the sequence 'as long as multiple threads are not running'; most algorithms and seeding functions may change across Python versions, but random() will produce the same sequence given the same seed with the compatible seeder.
limitations: Cross-version reproducibility not guaranteed for functions such as shuffle/sample; record Python version and seeds. Not for security use.
notes: Accessed 2026-10-04; page version 3.14.8.

title: networkx.algorithms.coloring.greedy_color
key_finding: Strategies: 'largest_first', 'random_sequential', 'smallest_last', 'independent_set', 'connected_sequential_bfs', 'connected_sequential_dfs', 'connected_sequential' (alias of dfs), 'saturation_largest_first', 'DSATUR' (alias of saturation_largest_first). interchange=True uses the colour-interchange algorithm of Syslo, Deo & Kowalik (1983); not compatible with saturation_largest_first or independent_set.
